prompt: A week has seven days and a year has twelve

units.explanation: Broad early head, measured on every token including the first. Predict plain English prose active-weak about one text in four, at 0.25-0.37 of max. Those peaks fall on the first to fourth token, for example on first tokens such as 'She', 'We', 'Our', 'My', 'Many', 'After', 'So', 'Yes' or 'Let', which alone reach 1.1-1.8. Predict non-English Latin-script prose (Turkish, Polish, Portuguese, German, Spanish) active on nearly every token. It is strongest (0.5-0.75 of max) on and after diacritic or byte-fragment tokens such as ' ç', 'ż', ' iç', 'ö' or 'ð', even when only one such word sits in an English sentence. The head is also strong (0.4-1.0) on the newline that ends a code or block-comment line when earlier lines began with the same indentation or ' *' token (it attends back to those tokens), and on chained ' -'/' +' operators in 'Let d(j) = 0 - j - 2*j - 9 + ...' arithmetic. The only class predicted inactive is a numbered English list item: a whole text made of one digit 1-9, a period, a space and one plain all-English sentence, 7-15 tokens in total (e.g. '4. The bridge was closed for repairs last summer.'). 27/27 such texts measured below the line, with a highest peak of 0.86 (0.19 of max). Short texts that lack this prefix (one-word sentences, word lists, integer lists) are NOT predicted inactive, and the prefix does not quiet non-English sentences.

Broad, mostly previous-token head: predict ordinary prose active-weak (most sentences of a dozen or more tokens have one or two tokens just over the line, roughly 10% of tokens, peaks near 0.3-0.45 of max), and it is strong (above ~0.6 of max) on a content word, or a later sub-word piece of a name or term, whose attention falls almost wholly (weight ~0.9) on the specifier opening its phrase: 'which' ('regardless of which system'), numerals ('the two Kivu'), 'every', 'any', possessives 'its'/'their', 'a' after a preposition ('At a global'), 'of' in 'some of / one of' before a name, 'are' in 'There are further', or the head noun before a name ('regional capital Białystok'); it is weak after 'the', 'this', 'that'. Comma lists of plain numbers and strings of one-word exclamations ('Stop. Yes! Okay?') are inactive.

L1/H6 is a broad copy head, not a detector: at every token it spreads attention over itself, the previous few words and a long tail of earlier context (mean weight 0.11 on itself, 0.12 on the previous token, the rest beyond that; it locks 0.8+ onto one token at only ~3% of positions) and writes that attention-weighted average of token values, so its strength |W_O(z-zbar)| is the distance of that average from its mean write and is large (1.0-3.0, 0.33-1.0 of max) exactly where the copy is dominated by a token far from the mean: demonstrative 'that'/'That is' (peak on the following word, 'that bill/town/letter/film' 1.0-2.5), 'this'/'these'/'Those' (0.7-1.7), expletive or subject 'it' (peak on the copula and adjective of 'it is / It has been X', 1.8-2.0), other pronouns ('I', 'you', 'we', 'they', 0.7-1.3) and rare content tokens such as proper nouns, money, unit and sports terms, split subwords and non-Latin-script words ('$2.4 billion', '247 yards', 'champion', 'Football', 1.0-3.0). Because nearly every text contains one such token, ordinary text of 8+ tokens is predicted active-weak somewhere (plain prose 22/25 measured at 0.78-2.31, median 1.06, usually on the noun after the determiner or the verb after the subject; even 4-6 token common-word sentences 7/8 at 0.67-1.9), and the only class that reliably stays below 0.25 x max is a bare comma-separated list of plain cardinal numbers - digits or number words, optional minus signs and decimal points, no other letters, no $ % = ; / or other symbols - which peaks at 0.0-0.41 (30/30 measured).

Broad induction-style head that is at most weakly active on ordinary prose without repeats, and fires strongly on the first or middle piece of a second or later occurrence of a rare multi-token word, repeated phrase, list-template bigram or paired code directive (second 'Tim' of a repeated 'Timmis', second ' ن' of a repeated ' نادي', the ',' before a repeated ' jquery', the '#' of '#endif' after '#ifdef'), attending back to the distinctive token that followed the earlier copy ('mis', 'اد', ' jquery', 'ifdef'). First-only mentions, repeated common words and parallel list items stay at most weakly active rather than strong, and isolated rare bytes ('�', BOM) are a small offshoot that can peak while attending to themselves.

Dense previous-token head that crosses the line on almost any text longer than a few tokens: strongest on the second piece of a word or name the tokenizer splits (Mac|mill, Mc|Av, bark|ed, cheer|ed), the token after ' there' ('s, is, be), an abbreviation's period, whitespace runs, list numbers, URLs and code, and it also crosses on the 2nd-4th tokens of any text that does not open with 'The' (A dog ate..., He kicked..., Mary won...) and on the token after ' and', ' on', ' over', ' near', ' all' or ' first'. It stays below the line only on (a) one single-token word followed by '.' ('Water.', 'Sorry.', 'True.') and (b) texts made only of 'The'-opened simple clauses of single-token everyday words, 'The N.', 'The N V.' or 'The N V the N.', one or several in a row, with no split word, adjective, preposition, 'and', comma, number, pronoun or name (known exceptions that still fire: ' door', ' way', ' other', ' same', ' time' after 'the').

Broad head: most ordinary prose and code crosses the active line weakly (about 0.8-1.7, often on a verb, preposition or 'and' shortly after the opener; 9 of 10 varied plain sentences and 7 of 20 'The N V ...' sentences crossed), so predict ordinary text active-weak. It is strong (above about 2.0) on the token one to four positions after a structural anchor that it attends to almost entirely: the day number and comma after a month name ('November 3,'), ' from' and the quote after 'import X', the '{' after '\frac', ';'/' without' after 'WARRANTY', '=' after 'Suppose 2*z'; predicted inactive (below 0.25 x max) is a whole text that is only a comma-and-space separated list of 5-8 plain integers 0-99 (9-15 tokens, no other words, e.g. '37, 2, 53, 71, 82, 12').

Broad previous-token head (about 0.9 of attention on token t-1) whose write departs from average according to what t-1 is: strong (1.5-3.6) inside any word the tokenizer splits into three or more pieces, on the pieces after a word-internal fragment (methyl|gly|ox|al, Q|iz|il|bash, val|v|opath|ies, Shost|ak|ovich, hex strings, German/Greek/Cyrillic words), and weak but usually over the line (0.9-1.8) on the token right after a short concrete noun, adjective or counted number in ordinary prose ('cat and', 'red car', '9 10', 'Tue ,'), so predict most English sentences that contain content nouns or adjectives active-weak. Predict inactive (peak below 0.5): text built only from pronouns, auxiliaries, determiners, prepositions, conjunctions and common verbs (say, know, think, do, go, want, have, be) with no content noun or adjective (e.g. 'It is not that I do not want to, it is that I cannot.'); one word repeated ('tree tree tree'); space-separated round numbers ('100 200 300'); and any two-token prompt, because positions 0 and 1 are always 0.

Broad previous-token head: predict ordinary prose, code and number lists active-weak (about 0.25-0.55 of max), but predict inactive a two-token text made of one lowercase common word that is a single token followed only by '.', '!' or '?' (e.g. 'cat.', 'road!', 'tree?'; capitalised words like 'Okay.' and words split into pieces like 'gar|den.' do not count). It is strong (above about 0.6 of max) on the second piece of a word split into sub-word tokens after a short, usually capitalised or all-caps, word-start fragment it attends to (GRE|ATER, PR|OT, PL|URAL, Cle|aring, Hod|ges, De Kal|b, CM|ake, url|pattern), and on fixed pairs such as Highway + route number, UPDATE ... SET and 'Story highlights'.

Broad layer-0 head: predict ordinary prose, code and names active-weak (content nouns, verbs and word fragments near a text's start reach 0.25-0.5 of max; a short plain sentence with no comma or determiner sits near the line, so about a third of those fall just below), and predict it strong (0.6-1.0 of max) on a comma or a determiner (' the', ' a', ' an') within roughly the first five tokens of a text, where it attends mostly to itself; the same tokens fade with position and are usually below the line by token 8-14. Predicted inactive (near 0): the tokens ' and', ' of', ' from', ' by' at any position, and short phrases whose every word is a single-token directional or adverb particle (Up, down, In, out, On, off, Over, under, Back, forth, around, again) joined only by ' and', ' of', ' from' or ' by' (e.g. 'Up and down', 'In and out of', 'Back and forth and back again', 'Up and down and all around'), with no comma, determiner, noun or multi-token word; pairs like 'Ahead and behind', 'Forward and backward', 'Left and right' or 'Near and far' are content or multi-token words and are predicted active-weak.

Phrase-frame head: it attends (weight >0.8) to one earlier token that opens the current phrase or line and writes on the 1-6 tokens after it. Strongest (0.5-1.0 of max) on a superlative noun phrase's head noun and the qualifier that follows it ('the largest forest [in]', 'the best player [on]', 'greatest driver [ever]', 'worst pain I've [ever]', 'busiest [nights]'), with 'most'/'-est'/'best'/'worst' attended. Weaker (0.25-0.6) on: 'first/only/last ... to' and comparatives ('the more ... the better you get', 'faster than anyone else in'); attribution after a closing quote (', she said'); code declaration bodies after func/class/private/#define; and templated lines repeated two or more times (math Q&A drills, answers after 'What is ...?\n', '(1887-1951),' name entries). Ordinary narrative prose, a single short sentence-initial clause, plain comma or number lists, and repeated names without a line template stay below 0.25 of max.

sections.title: What is explained and what is not
sections.text: The model answers ' days' where the right answer is ' months'. The verified answer experiment (VERIFIED, attempt 2) is a claim about this one prompt only. Separately, the first-order attribution on this prompt is mostly unexplained: the explained share is 0.0644 and the unexplained share is 0.9356 (blocked share 0.0041). Keeping the minimal set of 23 units (for example L2/H5, L3/H4, L1/H6, L3/H3, L0/N1877+, L0/N1277+, L0/N1101+, L3/N1350+, L4/H7, L5/H7) gives prompt coverage 0.938 against 0.101 for random units matched by kind and layer. Because coverage_caution is true, that coverage alone shows only that these units are sufficient on this prompt, not how they produce the answer. Heads alone reach 0.422 and poles alone 0.034, so the heads carry most of it. Ablating the 10 verified poles together changes the ' days' logit by only -0.017 and the top token stays ' days'. The route claim below, not the coverage figure, is what lets me say the answer is understood for this prompt.

sections.title: Step 1: the prompt marks two count words and a time unit
sections.text: The verified route starts from three source tokens: ' seven', ' days' and ' twelve'. Layer-0 count-word neurons (L0/N1877+, L0/N1277+, L0/N1108+, L0/N141+, L0/N1654+, L0/N1669+, L0/N195+, L0/N1866+, L0/N1944+, L0/N883+) fire on ' seven' and on the final ' twelve', which marks the last token as a bare count word that wants a counted noun. L0/N1277+ is the strongest single count marker at ' twelve'. Time-unit neurons (L0/N1101+, L0/N912+, L0/N2008+, L0/N780+) write the identity of ' days' at its position, the content that the copy heads later read. These roles come from the verified route claim.

sections.title: Step 2: early heads line up the two clauses
sections.text: L0/H0 builds the clause frame 'a <time unit> has <count>' at both clauses so they line up, and L0/H2 marks the start of each 'a X has' clause. L1/H1, L1/H3 and L1/H4 carry the clause and position frame forward, and L1/H1 is needed for the copy heads to find ' days' (sufficiency). L1/H7 writes 'count word after has' at ' seven' and ' twelve'. L1/H6 averages the earlier context (' week', ' seven', ' days') into later positions, which gives the query at ' twelve' the parallel-clause context. L3/N456+ re-marks ' twelve' as a count word in the middle layers. L1/H6 is a hub centre (percentile 0.25, not default-on), so it could be an artefact of its many links to studied units. The route claim still assigns it this role.

sections.title: Step 3: copying ' days' to the last position
sections.text: This is the core of the wrong answer. At ' twelve', the induction-style copy head L3/H3 attends to ' days', the token that followed the earlier count word ' seven', and writes ' days' to the last position. L4/H7 moves the ' days' identity to the last position after L3/H3, and L4/H0 reinforces that move. The model is therefore continuing the parallel clause by copying the noun that followed the first count word, not looking up what a year has twelve of. L3/N1350+ boosts the counted-noun prediction at the query position.

sections.title: Step 4: output neurons and why ' days' beats ' months'
sections.text: L5/H7 keeps the 'count word wants a noun' reading at the last position. L5/N1617+ pushes counted plural nouns such as ' days' up, and L5/N207+ pushes counted nouns up. L5/N2036-, L5/N575- and L5/N119- push layout and function tokens ('.', ',', ' and') down after the count word. According to the verified claim these layer-5 neurons do not choose between ' days' and ' months'. They only raise a counted noun in general, and the copied ' days' wins over the fact that a year has twelve months. So the model gets this wrong because the copy route puts ' days' at the last position and nothing in the verified route supplies or prefers ' months'.

sections.title: How well the route was tested
sections.text: The route has necessity 0.683, sufficiency 0.624 and patching 0.749. The reviewer's prompts came out as predicted in 20 of 24, and no gate failed. Per the claim: replacing ' twelve' with ' the' silences the count neurons, the copy does not fire and the answer leaves ' days'. Swapping the count word for another number keeps ' days', and swapping the copied noun makes the answer follow it. The route is a claim about this prompt only. Necessity and sufficiency of 0.68 and 0.62 also mean the route is not the whole story.

sections.title: Status of the other attributed units
sections.text: Several heads with large attribution here are VERIFIED, but only as scan-corpus descriptions, which may not cover this prompt: L2/H5 (broad early head), L3/H4 (previous-token head), L1/H2, L2/H1 and L0/H4 (previous-token heads), L3/H3 and L1/H6 (named above) and L1/H7. Their listed ablation changes are positive: L2/H5 0.975, L1/H6 0.724, L3/H4 0.341, L1/H7 0.242, L1/H2 0.197, L3/H3 0.138. Their attributions are mostly negative. The largest single attribution is L5/N2014+ (share 0.0066, attribution -1.35, ablation change +1.03). It is unstudied, so its role is not known, and it is not in the verified route. L1/H5 and L0/H6 are also unstudied. They have positive attribution and ablation changes of -0.83 and -0.66. L0/H6 appears in the paths as a source to L2/H5, L1/H2 and L1/H7, and L3/H3 appears as a source to L5/N2014+ (weight -0.32). I cannot say from this evidence what they do for ' days' versus ' months'.

sections.title: Not known yet and next experiments
sections.text: Not shown: why the model has no pull toward ' months' (the claim says layer-5 neurons do not choose, but the evidence has no unit that carries 'a year has twelve months'). Not shown: what L5/N2014+ does, since it has the largest share and is unstudied. Not shown: how much of the 0.9356 unexplained attribution the route covers, because the route's necessity (0.683) and sufficiency (0.624) are partial. Not shown: whether the route holds on other prompts. The listed next experiments are revising L1/N1994+ (coverage gain 0.0054), L4/N840+ (0.0045) and L4/N180+ (0.0032), which are NEEDS_REVISION, and exploring the unstudied L2/N1151+, L4/N1121+, L2/N1334+, L4/N863+, L2/N1016+, L5/H3 and L1/N1589+ (gains 0.0015 to 0.0022). Each gain is small, so none of them would explain much alone.

narration.paragraph: The model says ' days' because of a copy route that is VERIFIED for this prompt only. Layer-0 count-word neurons (L0/N1877+, L0/N1277+) mark ' seven' and ' twelve', time-unit neurons (L0/N1101+) write ' days', and early heads (L0/H0, L0/H2, L1/H1, L1/H3, L1/H4, L1/H6, L1/H7) line up the two 'a X has <count>' clauses. At ' twelve' the induction head L3/H3, with L4/H0 and L4/H7, copies ' days' (the noun after ' seven') to the last position. Layer-5 neurons (L5/N1617+, L5/N207+, L5/N2036-, L5/N575-, L5/N119-) raise counted nouns and lower layout tokens but do not choose between ' days' and ' months', so the copied ' days' wins. Necessity is 0.683, sufficiency 0.624, patching 0.749 and the reviewer prompts matched in 20 of 24. In first-order attribution only 0.0644 is explained and 0.9356 is not. The minimal set reaches coverage 0.938 against 0.101 for random units, but coverage_caution is true, so that shows sufficiency only. Not known: why nothing favours ' months', what the unstudied L5/N2014+ does, and whether the route holds on other prompts.
